passages.t: ‘Where is the promise of His coming?’
passages.happening:
“Beloved, this is now my second letter to you. Both of them are reminders to stir you to wholesome thinking by recalling what was foretold by the holy prophets and commanded by our Lord and Savior through your apostles” (verses 1-2).

“Most importantly, you must understand that in the last days scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires. ‘Where is the promise of His coming?’ they will ask. ‘Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation’” (verses 3-4).

“But they deliberately overlook the fact that long ago by God’s word the heavens existed and the earth was formed out of water and by water, through which the world of that time perished in the flood. And by that same word, the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men” (verses 5-7).
passages.hearers:
‘Beloved’ comes four times in this chapter. Peter writes with warmth, and with urgency. He calls the readers back to two witnesses he named in chapter 1: the prophets and the apostles.

Then the scoffers. Their mockery is a question: ‘Where is the promise of His coming?’ The first Christians had hoped Jesus might return soon. Years had passed, and some of the first believers had died; ‘fell asleep’ was a common Christian way of speaking of death. ‘The fathers’ may mean the first Christian leaders, or the patriarchs of Israel. Either way, the scoffers' point was: nothing has happened, so nothing will. The world goes on as it always has.

Many people in the Greek and Roman world believed the universe was stable and eternal, or turned in endless cycles. And a teaching that there will be no judgment suits people ‘following their own evil desires’.

Peter answers that the world has not always gone on unchanged. God's word made it, and God's word judged it in the flood. The same word now holds the present world ‘for fire’, for a day of judgment. History is not an endless circle. It is moving toward a day.

Peter is not giving a science lesson here. He speaks of creation and the flood to show that God has acted in the world before, and will again. These notes take no position on the age of the earth or on how widely the flood's waters spread. Christians who share the same faith differ on those questions, and Peter's point does not depend on them.
passages.ot:
Creation by God's word is the faith of the psalms: “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the stars by the breath of His mouth” (Psalm 33:6). In Genesis the earth comes out of the waters: “And God said, ‘Let there be an expanse between the waters, to separate the waters from the waters’” (Genesis 1:6).

And the flood is told as the waters returning: “all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the floodgates of the heavens were opened” (Genesis 7:11).

The prophets spoke of a day of fire: “For behold, the day is coming, burning like a furnace, when all the arrogant and every evildoer will be stubble” (Malachi 4:1).
passages.asks: Ask whether you, too, have quietly assumed that nothing will change. Ask whose voices, the prophets' and apostles' or the scoffers', shape what you expect. And ask how you would live differently if you believed that history is going somewhere.

passages.happening:
“Beloved, do not let this one thing escape your notice: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day. The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (verses 8-9).

“But the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Peter gives two more answers to the scoffers.

First, God does not count time as we do. ‘With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day.’ This echoes a psalm. It is about God's patience and his view of time. It is not a formula for working out dates, and Peter gives no date.

Second, what looks like slowness is patience. The word means ‘long-tempered’: able to act in anger, but holding back. God waits because he does not want people to perish. He wants them to turn. Many read this as God's sincere desire for every person to turn and live. Others, especially in the Reformed tradition, read such words in a narrower sense, as they read ‘who wants everyone to be saved’ in 1 Timothy 2:4, and the notes there set out how. Traditions explain these words differently, but all of them read them as sincere, and all agree that the time before Christ comes is a time of mercy.

Then: the day will come ‘like a thief’. A thief does not send word ahead. The picture comes from Jesus' own teaching, and the early church used it often for how suddenly he will come.

The rest of verse 10 is hard (see below). ‘The elements’ may mean the building blocks of the world, or the sun, moon and stars, which ancient writers also called by this word.
passages.ot:
Peter's line echoes Psalm 90: “For in Your sight a thousand years are but a day that passes, or a watch of the night” (Psalm 90:4).

God's patience and his wish that people turn are the message of the prophets: “As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked should turn from their ways and live” (Ezekiel 33:11).

‘The Day of the Lord’ is the prophets' name for the day God comes to judge: “The great Day of the LORD is near— near and coming quickly” (Zephaniah 1:14). And they pictured the heavens shaken: “All the stars of heaven will be dissolved. The skies will be rolled up like a scroll” (Isaiah 34:4).
passages.hard:
Will the earth be burned up and destroyed, or renewed? And what does ‘laid bare’ mean?

Here the manuscripts differ. Older translations followed later manuscripts that say the earth and its works ‘will be burned up’. Most modern translations follow early manuscripts that have a word meaning ‘will be found’, which the BSB renders ‘the earth and its works will be laid bare’. On that reading, the fire of judgment exposes everything to God's sight, rather than simply wiping it out.

Christians have taken two main views. Some read the passage as teaching that the present universe will be wholly destroyed and replaced by a new creation. Others read it as a purging fire that refines and renews the present creation, much as the flood, the comparison Peter himself makes in verse 6, judged the world without abolishing the earth. They point to Romans 8:19-23, where creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay. These notes do not choose.

Both views agree on Peter's point. The present order is not permanent. Everything will be judged. And God's promise is a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells. Peter gives no timetable, and these notes offer no scheme of the last days.
passages.asks: Ask whether you have mistaken God's patience for slowness, or for absence. Ask whom you know who needs time to turn, and pray for them. And ask what in your life would be ‘laid bare’ before God today.

passages.t: What kind of people ought you to be?
passages.happening:
“Since everything will be destroyed in this way, what kind of people ought you to be? You ought to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness as you anticipate and hasten the coming of the day of God, when the heavens will be destroyed by fire and the elements will melt in the heat. But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells” (verses 11-13).

“Therefore, beloved, as you anticipate these things, make every effort to be found at peace—spotless and blameless in His sight. Consider also that our Lord’s patience brings salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote you with the wisdom God gave him. He writes this way in all his letters, speaking in them about such matters. Some parts of his letters are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction” (verses 14-16).
passages.hearers:
Peter's question is the point of the whole chapter. If the present world is not permanent, ‘what kind of people ought you to be?’ His answer is not to make charts of the end or to withdraw from the world. It is to live holy and godly lives, at peace, spotless and blameless.

‘Anticipate and hasten’ is striking. Believers do not only wait; Peter says they ‘hasten’ the day. He does not explain how, and it is wise not to say more than he does.

And the hope is not a far-off heaven of spirits only. It is ‘a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells’. Righteousness will be at home there, not a guest.

Then Peter mentions Paul, ‘our beloved brother’. Paul, too, wrote of God's patience leading people to turn: “do you disregard the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?” (Romans 2:4). Peter admits that some parts of Paul's letters are ‘hard to understand’, a sentence many readers since have found comforting. And he warns that ignorant and unstable people twist them, ‘as they do the rest of the Scriptures’.

That last phrase is one of the earliest signs that Paul's letters were being read as Scripture. It also shows they were already being bent to suit people's wishes.
passages.ot:
The new heaven and new earth are Isaiah's promise: “For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth. The former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind” (Isaiah 65:17). And, “For just as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, will endure before Me” (Isaiah 66:22).

A world where righteousness is at home is pictured in the psalm: “righteousness and peace have kissed” (Psalm 85:10). And Isaiah: “They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water” (Isaiah 11:9).
passages.hard:
‘Some parts of his letters are hard to understand.’ If Scripture can be hard, and can be twisted, how should ordinary readers read it?

Peter does not say that Scripture is too hard for ordinary people. He says that some parts are hard, and that the danger comes when ‘ignorant and unstable’ people distort them. The answer is not to stop reading. It is to read humbly, slowly, and together.

That means reading a hard verse in the light of the whole letter and the whole Bible, not pulling it out to prove a point. It means reading with others, past and present, and being willing to be corrected. And it means being honest when a passage is hard, as Peter is about Paul.

The notes on this site try to do that: to set out the main readings where faithful Christians differ, and to say plainly when something is hard. Where readers differ, read more than one view before you settle, and hold your own view as one who may yet be taught.
passages.asks: Ask what kind of person you are becoming while you wait. Ask whether you look forward to the new heaven and earth, or only fear the end of this one. And ask whether you read hard passages of Scripture humbly, or bend them to say what you already think.

passages.happening: “Therefore, beloved, since you already know these things, be on your guard so that you will not be carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your secure standing. But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen” (verses 17-18).
passages.hearers:
The letter ends with a warning and a call. The warning: you know these things, so be on guard. Do not be swept away by people who live without God's law. The call: grow.

‘Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.’ The letter began with knowledge (1:2) and ends with it. Knowledge here is not secret information. It is knowing Christ, and it grows as grace grows.

The last words give glory to Jesus Christ ‘both now and to the day of eternity’. This is praise the Bible elsewhere gives to God alone, a quiet confession, at the end, of what the letter said at the start: Jesus is ‘our God and Savior’ (1:1).
passages.ot:
The psalms often end in praise, as this letter does: “Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and amen” (Psalm 89:52).

And growth is the psalm's picture of the righteous: “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon” (Psalm 92:12).
passages.asks: Ask what might carry you away from your secure standing, and how you can be on guard against it. Ask whether you are growing in knowing Christ, or only in knowing about him. And end where Peter ends: give him glory.
